blurb: How chips are made: from sand to ultra-pure silicon, printing with light, tiny switch shapes, and why it's all geopolitics.

steps.h: What a chip is made of
steps.p: A chip is billions of transistors — microscopic on/off switches — built on silicon, a material made from sand.
steps.analogy: Each transistor is like a tap: it lets electricity flow or stops it. Billions of taps switching on and off do all the computing.

steps.p: Sand is refined into silicon so pure that only about one atom in a billion is anything else.
A seed crystal is dipped into molten silicon and slowly pulled out, growing a single perfect crystal about 2 metres long.
The crystal is sliced into thin discs 300 mm across — wafers — and polished mirror-smooth. Hundreds of chips are built on each.
Adding tiny amounts of other atoms (doping) controls how silicon conducts. Phosphorus adds spare electrons; boron creates gaps. That's what makes switches possible.

cards.q: What size wafers do the most advanced chip factories use?
cards.why: 300 mm — about the size of a dinner plate. Bigger wafers fit more chips per batch.

cards.statement: A transistor is basically a switch that electricity can turn on and off.
cards.why: True. A small voltage on one terminal lets current flow (on) or blocks it (off). Every calculation is built from billions of these.

cards.q: Adding phosphorus atoms to silicon makes it…
cards.why: n-type. Phosphorus brings one extra electron that's free to move. Boron does the opposite, making "p-type".

cards.title: Chip-grade silicon is about 99.9999999% pure — "nine nines".
cards.detail: That's roughly one foreign atom per billion silicon atoms. Even tiny traces of metal at this level can ruin transistors.

cards.statement: Moore's law is a law of physics.
cards.why: False. It's an observation from 1965 that transistor counts doubled roughly every two years — kept going by huge engineering effort, and slowing.

steps.p: The wafer is coated with light-sensitive chemical. Light shines through a stencil (a mask), and where it hits, the chemical changes.
steps.analogy: Like developing an old photo, or a sun print.

steps.p: The changed areas are washed away, and the exposed silicon is etched or filled with material — copying the pattern.
A modern chip needs dozens of these layers stacked precisely on top of each other.
Finer lines need shorter wavelengths of light. The latest machines use extreme ultraviolet (EUV) at 13.5 nanometres — thousands of times thinner than a hair.

visual.caption: Wavelength of light used: shorter is finer.

steps.p: EUV light is absorbed by glass and even air, so the machines use ultra-smooth mirrors in a vacuum.

cards.q: EUV lithography uses light with a wavelength of about…
cards.why: 13.5 nm. Shorter light can draw finer lines, like a sharper pencil. The older deep-ultraviolet machines used 193 nm light.

cards.q: Which company is the only supplier of EUV machines?
cards.why: ASML, from the Netherlands. Each machine costs well over $100 million and is the size of a bus.

cards.statement: EUV light passes through glass lenses just like visible light.
cards.why: False. Glass absorbs it, so the machines use special mirrors inside a vacuum.

cards.title: EUV light is made by hitting tiny drops of molten tin with a laser about 50,000 times a second.
cards.detail: Each drop is struck twice — once to flatten it, once to blast it into a glowing plasma that gives off 13.5 nm light.

cards.statement: The "3 nm" in a "3 nm chip" is the actual size of its transistors.
cards.why: False. It's a marketing label for a generation. The real features are bigger; the number just signals "newer and denser".

cards.title: From flat to fins to wrap-around

steps.p: Early transistors were flat. As they shrank, the control part (the gate) could no longer fully stop current — they leaked even when "off".
steps.analogy: A tap so small it can't fully close, so it always drips.

steps.p: From 2011, the channel became a thin vertical fin, with the gate wrapped around three sides — much better control.
The newest transistors use stacked sheets with the gate surrounding them on every side.
Around 2005, shrinking transistors stopped saving power in proportion, so chips got hotter. Speeds stalled at a few GHz and chips added more cores instead.
NVIDIA's H100 has about 80 billion transistors. Its successor joins two chips to exceed 200 billion.

cards.q: What mainly forced the move away from flat transistors?
options: Leakage — the gate could no longer fully switch them off
They were too expensive to draw
cards.why: Leakage. Wrapping the gate around more sides gives it a firmer grip on the channel.

cards.q: When shrinking transistors stopped saving power in the mid-2000s…
options: Clock speeds stalled, and chips added more cores instead
cards.why: Speeds stalled. Running faster made chips too hot, so designers used extra transistors for more cores.

cards.statement: Intel was the first company to ship FinFET transistors in volume.
cards.why: True. In its 22 nm chips in 2011–12. TSMC and Samsung followed a few years later.

cards.title: NVIDIA's H100 GPU packs about 80 billion transistors onto one chip.
cards.detail: Its Blackwell successor exceeds 200 billion by joining two chips, each as large as manufacturing machines can print in one go.

cards.q: "Backside power delivery" moves which wiring underneath the transistors?
cards.why: Power wires. Moving them below frees room above for data wiring and delivers power more efficiently.

steps.p: Companies like NVIDIA, Apple and AMD design chips but don't own factories — they're "fabless".
TSMC in Taiwan makes most of the world's most advanced chips. Samsung and Intel are the only other leading-edge makers.
Specialised suppliers from the Netherlands, Japan and the US make the machines and chemicals — including ASML's EUV machines.
AI chips are packaged with HBM memory side by side on a shared base (TSMC's CoWoS). This step became a major shortage.
Because so much depends on a few companies and places, chips are now a matter of national security, with export controls and huge subsidies.

cards.q: Which of these companies is "fabless" — designs chips but doesn't make them?
cards.hint: Look at the flow in step 3.
cards.why: NVIDIA. It designs GPUs and pays TSMC to manufacture them. Apple and AMD work the same way.

cards.statement: Most of the world's most advanced chips are made in Taiwan.
cards.why: True. TSMC's Taiwanese factories produce the large majority of leading-edge chips, which is why the island matters so much strategically.

cards.q: TSMC's CoWoS packaging became a bottleneck for AI chips. What does it do?
options: Places GPU chips and HBM memory side by side on a shared base
cards.why: Puts GPU and memory together. Placing them close allows the huge memory speeds AI needs — but capacity was limited.

cards.title: A single leading-edge chip factory costs over $20 billion to build.
cards.detail: Ultra-clean rooms, EUV machines and hundreds of other tools drive the price — which is why only three companies compete at the frontier.

cards.statement: Since 2022, the US has restricted exports of top AI GPUs and chipmaking tools to China.
cards.why: True. The rules have been tightened several times, pushing China to develop its own chips and tools.
